## 1.0 Introduction

Across the world, sea level rise is accelerating, threatening coastal habitats worldwide through loss of terrestrial space (cite here explaining scope of threatening of coastal habitats). Coastal habitats are important, transitional ecosystems that provide access to terrestrial and aquatic resources (cite here significance ecologically of coastal habitats). They also provide a buffer to terrestrial systems and human communities from flood risk (@taylor-burns2024). Sea level rise directly threatens the services and the unique ecosystems that are provided by coastal habitats.

Salt marshes are coastal habitats that hold significant importance as the hosts for endemic organisms that depend on the conditions that only salt marshes provide, such as tidal inundation, soil composition, and drainage processes (need a citation here to explain the specific traits of the marsh and what it has to offer). However, salt marshes are at risk of elimination through a threefold problem: lateral coastal squeeze through human development across the coast line (need a citation here about coastal squeeze's threat to marshes), sea level rise is rising at an accelerating rate ( @thorne, other studies in other locations that talk about SLR in regards to marshes), and the available sediment supply in the water column isn’t enough for marshes to rise vertically on pace with sea level rise due to up river damming of systems ( cite Sediment for Survival, other studies that have talked about damming of rivers in other areas ). These problems underline the urgency to understand basic processes of how marshes build over time, as well as the individual factors that influence those processes ( cite multiple papers that have attempted to isolate explanatory factors and processes-erosion/prograding, accreting, etc). One of these processes includes sediment deposition, which is the single event of sediment in the water flooding over the marsh, and the sediment settles onto the marsh platform (basic citation of process?). This can occur during a high tide event when the water level can overtop the marsh edge and flood the platform (Figure 1).

As Figure 1 above demonstrates, the processes of deposition can vary across space within a single marsh across different tidal scales ( @leonardi2018, also additional papers that talk about sediment deposition). To further complicate matters, each of these factors frequently confound with each other ( @taylor-burns2023, @foster-martinez2018, cite here about how vegetation effects sediment deposition). The abiotic factor of waves interacts with the vegetation as waves interact with the marsh edge. The vegetation could create an obstacle to slow down the water as it moves through the marsh ( @foster-martinez2018, @taylor-burns2023, @nederhoff2021), there again creating a new opportunity for the sediment to fall through the water column to the marsh platform. However, this biotic factor is also influenced through the abiotic factors of seasonality and toleration to humidity and salinity, where the biomass present on the marsh platform that provides a structure could be diminished in the non-growing season or different inundation levels, thereby decreasing the amount of time for the marsh platform is exposed to slow moving water with a greater opportunity for sediment to settle out (citation here). To understand the full processes of sediment deposition, research must incorporate the unique temporal and spatial scales of the marsh.

Across time, seasonality plays a strong factor in differences of deposition, such as wind fetch and wave power (citation here). Seasonality could also change how much sediment is washed away through the watershed to the marshes as available sediment to be deposited onto the marsh surface (@christiansen2000). When measuring the same marsh on a multi-year scale, observed differences in seasonality and weather patterns could result in even greater comparable differences in sediment deposition ( @fettweis1998, @thorne2013, @schoellhamer).

Within the space of a marsh, elevation and distance from the marsh edge have been pointed out as strong factors influencing sediment deposition in a marsh (cite). These factors can vary within a single marsh, making it hard to entangle how rates of sediment deposition can be modeled for a full marsh habitat to adapt to sea level rise (cite). Additionally, vegetation differences throughout the marsh as described earlier can influence the speed and time inundated of water can flow over the marsh platform (cite). These factors have been explored that influence vertical growth of the marsh, influencing marsh accretion over time (cite).

The structural features of the marsh edge include the shape of the marsh edge. An abiotic factor, such as waves hit interact with this shape of the marsh edge on a flooding tide could potentially affect the speed of the water as it floods across the marsh platform (@beaglejrsalomonmbaumgartensagrossingerrm.2015), which could accelerate sediment deposition rates. However, as can be seen from Figure 2, the scarped shape of a marsh edge could collapse some of the marsh platform from the force of the waves and imbalance of proportions (@fagherazzi2020 , @möller2002 ). Scarped marsh edges are commonly signals of an eroding marsh edge. Lateral and vertical movement of the marsh are both important metrics of marsh health. Few studies have incorporated both the means of lateral movement (marsh edge change) and vertical movement (short term sediment deposition) together into one study to understand how these factors near the marsh edge converge. ( @fagherazzi2020).

Within the San Francisco Bay Estuary, multiple studies have measured and predicted how sediment deposition has varied across space (@winklerprins2024, @lacy2020, @beaglejrsalomonmbaumgartensagrossingerrm.2015, @sfei), seasonally ( @lacy2018, @foster-martinez2018), and across years (@thorne2024). Comparing the findings of these studies underlines the complexity and nuance of each marsh’s components regarding sediment deposition as a process (cite different temporal and spatial scopes of studies when they've combined them together).

As SLR continues to threaten the existence of salt marshes, it is important to study both how sediment deposits vertically through short term deposition with a consideration of the unique space of the marsh features ( @willemsen2022, @hopkinson2018) as the marsh builds laterally. The focus of this study is to understand how short-term sediment deposition can vary across characterized marsh edge types. In this study, short-term sediment deposition rates were measured monthly at four different marshes within the northern San Francisco Bay Estuary for 12-months (Figure 3).

Four marshes within the Estuary were chosen based on their unique position and their marsh edge type. Two of the marshes, Corte Madera Ecological Reserve and Giant Marsh, studied had an identified “Scarp” edge shape, and two of the marshes, San Pablo National Wildlife Refuge (NWR) and Buck’s Landing, studied had an identified “Ramped” edge. Sediment deposition was measured throughout all the sites, in an attempt to understand three research questions: (1) How does sediment deposition rate vary across marsh edge types for one year? (2) Are sediment deposition rates in the same marsh edge type consistent across years? , (3) Are the factors influencing the rates of sediment deposition unique within each marsh?

This study fills a need to understand both processes of vertical and lateral movement of the marsh edge so that managers and scientists can better adapt to different rates of change at the marsh edge with expected SLR.
